content: The groups did not show any significant differences at the 6-month mark, and the changes observed between baseline and 6 months were not significantly different between the groups. However, baseline outcomes indicated that the fortified milk group had a higher potential for greater improvement. The evidence was downgraded by two levels due to concerns about study quality. The study by Stekel (1986) was assessed as having a high risk of bias because blinding was not reported. One trial (Villalpando) reported on this outcome, but no significant differences were observed between groups at 6 months, nor were there significant changes from baseline to 6 months between the groups. Five trials (Stekel 1986, Stekel 1988, Svahn 1999, Szynmlek-Gay, and Villalpando 2006) reported on this outcome. The evidence was downgraded by two levels due to the lack of randomization and blinding in some studies, as well as the high risk of bias. Additionally, blinding of outcome assessment was not mentioned, leading to a further downgrade of evidence by one level. Another level of downgrade was applied due to the small sample sizes in both the control and intervention groups. The trial by Stekel (1988) did not report on the blinding of participants, personnel, or outcome assessment, leading to a downgrade of evidence by one level. The small sample size in both the intervention and control groups resulted in an additional downgrade of evidence. The study by Akkermans (2016) was a double-blind, randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted across multiple countries with two arms. Participants included children aged 12–36 months with stable health status from Germany, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom. The intervention involved follow-on formula, and outcomes included serum ferritin levels, prevalence of iron deficiency (ID) and iron deficiency anemia (IDA), nutrient intakes, weight, height, weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ), height-for-age z-scores (HAZ), iron deficiency, and stool characteristics. The study was supported by Danone Nutrition Research, and the products were provided and coded by Nutricia Cuijk. Random sequence generation was assessed as low risk due to the use of a computer model for block randomization with stratification by country and sex. Allocation concealment was unclear. Baseline outcome measurements and characteristics were comparable among groups, except for differences in parental education, working status, iron intake, and vitamin D intake. Blinding of participants, personnel, and outcome assessment was adequately performed, and statistical analyses were finalized before unblinding. The study was registered at the Clinical Trial Registry of the Netherlands. The study by Bhatnagar (1996) was an RCT with two arms, involving children aged 3–24 months with diarrhea lasting at least 14 days but less than 12 weeks. Participants were recruited from diarrhea treatment units in New Delhi, India, between February 1992 and January 1995. The intervention included a milk-based cereal dietary regimen. Random sequence generation was assessed as low risk due to the use of stratified randomization with permutation blocks. Allocation concealment was also assessed as low risk, as the randomization list was centrally managed and provided to investigators by an independent person. Baseline outcome measurements and characteristics were similar between groups. Incomplete outcome data were addressed, with data included up to the time of withdrawal for outcomes other than treatment failure and weight change. Blinding of participants, personnel, and outcome assessment was unclear. The study was supported by the Diarrheal Diseases Control Programme of the World Health Organization. The study by Brunser (1993) was a prospective cohort study with two arms, conducted in a low socioeconomic community in Santiago, Chile. Children were divided into two groups: one received iron-fortified milk, and the other received control milk. Each cohort was followed for 6 months. Outcomes included the incidence of diarrhea, bowel movements, stool characteristics, and asymptomatic shedding of enteropathogens. The fortified milk contained 12 mg/L of iron, while the control milk contained 1 mg/L. Random sequence generation, allocation concealment, and baseline outcome measurements were unclear. Incomplete outcome data, blinding of participants, personnel, and outcome assessment, and selective reporting were also unclear. The study by Chatchatee (2014) was a double-blind, multi-country RCT with three arms, involving healthy children aged 11–29 months attending daycare centers. The study was conducted in Malaysia, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, and Thailand. Participants were randomly assigned to receive follow-on formula with added short-chain galacto-oligosaccharides (scGOS), long-chain fructo-oligosaccharides (lcFOS), and long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 LCPUFAs); control follow-on formula without these additions; or cow’s milk (reference group). Outcomes included episodes of respiratory and gastrointestinal infections, symptoms, and medication use. The study was supported by Danone Research, and the products were packed in identical tins to ensure blinding. Random sequence generation was assessed as low risk, but allocation concealment was unclear. Baseline outcome measurements and characteristics were comparable between groups. Incomplete outcome data were addressed, and blinding of participants, personnel, and outcome assessment was adequately performed. The study was registered at the Clinical Trial Registry of the Netherlands. However, the reference group using cow’s milk was not randomized, and the study was not included in the meta-analysis.
